Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

Every style is a space with rules. You can combine inside it, explore it, or change one of its rules.

Creativity is the ability to come up with ideas or artefacts that are new, surprising and valuable.

(Boden 2004, 1)

Image: A colour plate from Owen Jones's Grammar of Ornament (1868): a page of Moorish tile patterns, each one a different variation built from the same geometric rules.

Grammar of Ornament, plate XLIII: Moresque No. 5 · Owen Jones · Public domain · Source

Read the style

Before theory: pick one piece of design. What are its rules? Which rule held, and which one changed?

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

Language · medium · support

Language: the style and its rules. Medium: the material, which has rules too. Support: where the work lives, and who decides it is valuable.

many arguments about creativity are rooted in disagreements about value.

(Boden 2004, 10)

Image: A hand-coloured fashion plate from La Mode Illustrée (1880): two women in bustle dresses, one teal, one purple, standing in a salon beside a window.

La Mode Illustrée, 1880, No. 22: Toilettes de Mon. Fladry · La Mode Illustrée (publisher); Rijksmuseum (CC0) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Language = the style's grammar; today we call it a conceptual space.
  • Medium = material and technique: it makes some moves easy, others nearly impossible.
  • Support = magazine, shop, feed, jury: who gets to call it valuable.
  • Then: which road did the piece take — combine, explore or transform? Name the rule.

Source: (Boden 2004, 10)

Ask: Who decided this 1880 dress was in fashion — the maker, the magazine, or the buyer?

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

1 · New, surprising, valuable — new to whom?

P-creative: new to you. H-creative: new to history. For a student, P-creativity is the one that counts.

P–creativity involves coming up with a surprising, valuable idea that’s new to the person who comes up with it.

(Boden 2004, 2)

Image: Albert Anker's 1888 painting of a young girl standing at a table, knitting, with a basket of yarn on her arm.

Strickendes Mädchen (Girl Knitting) · Albert Anker · Public domain · Source

  • New, surprising, valuable: all three.
  • Everyone is creative to a degree — not a rare gift.
  • Ask how creative, and in which way, not yes or no.

Source: (Boden 2004, 1–2)

Ask: Name an idea you had that turned out to be old. Did it stop being creative for you?

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

2 · A style is a space you can map

A conceptual space is a style of thinking with rules — in music, science, or couture. You pick it up from your culture.

Conceptual spaces are structured styles of thought.

(Boden 2004, 4)

Image: John Ogilby's 1675 strip road map: the route from London to Bristol drawn as seven vertical scrolls, with side roads, towns and compass roses.

The Road from London to the City of Bristol (1675) · John Ogilby · Public domain · Source

  • Boden's list includes fashions in couture and choreography.
  • No single person invents a space; you learn it from a group.
  • Later she calls these maps of the mind: they guide thought into some paths and not others.

Source: (Boden 2004, 4; 59)

Ask: Write three rules of a style everyone in this room would recognise.

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

3 · Three roads: combine, explore, transform

Combine familiar ideas in a new way. Explore what a style can already do. Or transform it by changing a rule.

The first involves making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas.

(Boden 2004, 3)

Image: An American crazy quilt from about 1880: dozens of irregular silk and velvet patches in reds and browns, stitched together into one surface.

Crazy Quilt · Unknown American maker; The Metropolitan Museum of Art (photograph, CC0) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Combination needs a link people can follow; random is not enough.
  • Exploration shows possibilities you had not glimpsed.
  • Transformation makes the 'impossible' idea possible by changing the style.

Source: (Boden 2004, 3–6)

Ask: This quilt — which road? What would a transformed quilt look like?

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

4 · Rules are the material of change

No rules means no style to change. Negate a rule, drop it, or ask what it is for. You can only break a rule you know.

far from being the antithesis of creativity, constraints on thinking are what make it possible.

(Boden 2004, 95)

Image: Two line diagrams from 1866: a single hexagon ring of six carbon atoms, and a larger linked ring structure, as proposed by August Kekulé.

Benzene structures proposed by Kekulé in 1866 · August Kekulé · Public domain · Source

  • Consider the negative: applied to a deep rule, it can redraw the space in one step.
  • Schoenberg dropped even the home-chord ending and left tonality.
  • Perkins: ask not how it is usually done but what it is supposed to do.
  • To recognise a structural novelty, you need a structured mind.

Source: (Boden 2004, 66; 72; 74; 95), (Perkins 1995, 103)

Ask: Which rule of your current project have you never questioned?

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

5 · The critics: search, systems, process

Perkins: creative work is search, and it gets stuck in four ways. Ram and colleagues: the map shows creativity is possible, not how it works.

Problems are hard creatively when the circumstances mask novel solutions.

(Perkins 1995, 108)

Image: Jean-Simon Berthélemy's 1767 painting: Alexander in armour raises his sword over the knot while soldiers and priests crowd around.

Alexander Cuts the Gordian Knot · Jean-Simon Berthélemy · Public domain · Source

  • Perkins: creative systems = anything that yields adaptive novelty (minds, teams, evolution, cultures).
  • Four traps: rarity, isolation, oasis (almost good), plateau (no direction). Only isolation needs a bigger space.
  • Perkins: Boden underplays creative results from systems that never change their rules.
  • Ram et al.: the book leaves most process details unexplained — but shows an explanation is possible.

Source: (Perkins 1995, 98–108), (Ram et al. 1995, 111)

Ask: Last time you were stuck — oasis or plateau?

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

6 · Ordinary minds, practised — value is argued

Big ideas come from ordinary thinking, used with knowledge and control. Practice changes the space you search. Who judges the value stays open.

Great leaps do not come from extraordinary thinking. They come from ordinary thinking used extraordinarily well.

(Tao of Creativity)

Image: A page of Hokusai's sketchbook Manga: travellers under wide straw umbrellas, a porter with a pole and a rider on a horse, drawn in quick, sure lines.

Hokusai Manga, volume I (page) · Katsushika Hokusai · Public domain · Source

  • Ram et al.: extraordinary outcomes from ordinary mechanisms plus strategic control.
  • Design team example: a submarine launching missiles one at a time → launch each egg separately.
  • Ideas move from one design culture to another.
  • Expertise changes the search space and how you search it.
  • Boden: values change and are disputed; with image-evolving programs, a person still picks what survives.

Source: (Ram et al. 1995, 112; 116; 117; 126), (Boden 2004, 9–10)

Ask: If a program makes the variants and you pick one, who is the author?

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

Recall check

Alone, from memory, 3 minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. What three things make an idea creative, for Boden?
  2. What is the difference between P- and H-creativity?
  3. Name the three roads to a creative idea.
  4. Name one move that can change a rule of a conceptual space.
  5. What do Ram and colleagues say Boden's book leaves unexplained?

Course geometric background · feedback · #86525d56 · Original course SVG

Answers:

  • 1. New, surprising and valuable (Boden 2004, 1).
  • 2. P: new to the person who has it; H: new in human history (Boden 2004, 2).
  • 3. Combination, exploration, transformation (Boden 2004, 3).
  • 4. Consider the negative (Boden 2004, 66); drop a constraint (Boden 2004, 72); ask what it is for (Perkins 1995, 103).
  • 5. Most details of the processes of creativity and how they interact (Ram et al. 1995, 111).

Lab · Map it, then change it

Two exercises come next. Everything you produce in Lab goes into your portfolio index.

Save the rule list, the sketches, the changed rule and the partner's answers.

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

Exercise 1 · Map a style, then explore it

Write six rules of a style you know. Sketch three variants that keep every rule, then one that joins a distant field — and write the link.

Student: Does my idea count if history had it first? Master: The moon is not less full when seen through leaves — but do you see the gaps where the light passes?

(Tao of Creativity)

Six-rule list, four thumbnails, one road label (explore / combine) per thumbnail.

Image: A brown-ink sheet by Luigi Baccio del Bianco (about 1620): seven heads, each wearing a different fantastical hat on the same basic shape.

Seven Designs for Hats · Luigi Baccio del Bianco; The Metropolitan Museum of Art (photograph, CC0) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Timer: 25 minutes, pairs.
  • Rules: shape, material, colour, type or pattern, user, place.
  • Three variants keep every rule (explore); one joins a distant field (combine) with a written link.
  • Keep the rule list for Exercise 2.

Master Lecture · Conceptual Spaces and Creative Change

Exercise 2 · Change one rule

Circle the most fixed rule. Negate it, drop it, or ask what it is for. Sketch one variant, then add one new rule. Swap: new? surprising? valuable — to whom?

A rule, not a cage — an anchor you can lift once when you know the sea.

(Tao of Creativity)

Circled rule, the move used, the new sketch, the replacement rule, the other pair's three answers, one oasis-or-plateau sentence.

Image: Piet Mondrian's 1911 painting Gray Tree: a tree reduced to black curving branches over a grey ground, halfway between a real tree and a pattern of lines.

Gray Tree · Piet Mondrian · Public domain · Source

  • Timer: 25 minutes, same pairs.
  • One move only: negate, drop, or function question.
  • Step 4 replaces the broken rule so the new space still has a shape.
  • Last line: before the change, were you on an oasis or a plateau?

Carry forward

For your project: one rule of its space you will keep, and one rule you will test. Write it in your portfolio index.
